summary: Defines a schema for LDAP-based agents and a proposed use for it, distributed configuration of similar directory user agents. It proposes a set of attribute types and an object class so agents can learn where directory data lives and how to reach it. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Programs that look things up in a directory need settings. This note shows how to keep those settings in the directory itself so all similar programs can read the same ones.

questions: what is the ldap configuration profile schema
how to configure ldap clients from a directory
how do ldap agents configure themselves
what attributes are in the dua config profile
subtitle: A shared configuration schema for LDAP-based agents to discover directory settings.

tldr.problem: Different LDAP applications define their own schemas and configuration methods, causing data redundancy and making it hard to manage multiple similar agents across a network.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a standard set of attributes and an object class (DUAConfigProfile) that LDAP agents can read from the directory to learn how to access directory data, what schema to use, and how to authenticate.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now configure themselves from a central location in the directory, reducing redundancy and simplifying management of LDAP agents across platforms.

today: RFC 4876 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It remains a useful blueprint for LDAP client configuration. While not universally adopted, it is used in production systems, especially in environments where centralized management of many LDAP agents across multiple platforms is needed.

sections.title: The Configuration Problem for LDAP Agents
sections.content:
Many different applications act as LDAP clients, looking up information in directory servers. These applications include email services, authentication systems, and naming services. Each application traditionally defines its own configuration, even though they are doing similar things like connecting to a directory and searching for data.

The problem is that this leads to two challenges. First, different applications use different schema elements for the same kinds of data, causing administrators to store redundant information in the directory. Second, manually configuring many LDAP agents across a network, especially on different operating systems, becomes a significant management burden.

This RFC proposes a solution: a standard configuration schema that any LDAP agent can use to configure itself from the directory. Instead of hardcoding connection details and schema mappings, an agent can read a configuration profile from the directory itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of it like this: programs that look things up in a directory need to know where the directory is and how to talk to it. This RFC says: instead of telling each program separately, put the instructions in the directory itself so all programs can read them.

sections.title: The DUAConfigProfile Schema
sections.content:
At the core of this RFC is the DUAConfigProfile object class, which represents a configuration profile for a directory user agent (DUA). This object class is composed of attributes that cover three main areas: server connection details, search configuration, and authentication settings.

The RFC defines 16 attributes that can be part of a configuration profile. These include preferredServerList and defaultServerList for specifying which directory servers to contact (in order of preference). Other key attributes include defaultSearchBase for where to start searches, authenticationMethod for how to authenticate to the directory, and credentialLevel for what credentials to use.

The schema is designed to be extensible: implementers can add service-specific attributes in auxiliary object classes that combine with DUAConfigProfile to create profiles tailored to specific applications.
sections.plainLanguage: The configuration object is like a form that stores: where to find the directory, how to log in, what to search for, and how to handle the data you find. Different programs can add their own fields to this form for their specific needs.

sections.title: Key Configuration Attributes
sections.content:
The preferredServerList and defaultServerList attributes contain whitespace-separated lists of directory servers and port numbers. The agent first tries servers in the preferred list in order, then falls back to the default list if needed. This supports high availability: multiple servers should contain replicated data.

The serviceSearchDescriptor attribute is particularly powerful for handling schema variation. It allows specifying search base, scope, and filter for individual services, supporting multiple search locations within the directory tree. This means agents can find data spread across the directory even when schemas differ.

The attributeMap and objectclassMap attributes solve the core schema consistency problem. They let an agent map attributes or classes that the application expects to the names and classes actually in the deployed directory. For example, if a service expects an attribute called 'cn' but the directory uses 'employeeName', the map bridges the difference.
sections.plainLanguage: These attributes act like a translator and a map. The translator converts the application's expected field names into what's actually in the directory. The map tells the agent: 'Try this server first, then that one if the first is down.'

sections.title: How Agents Interpret the Configuration
sections.content:
When an LDAP agent starts, it reads a DUAConfigProfile entry from the directory. The agent uses the authenticationMethod attribute to determine the order of authentication methods to try, such as simple bind, SASL, or TLS with encryption. The credentialLevel attribute specifies whether to authenticate as an anonymous user, as a proxy identity, or as the current user.

The RFC defines a specific algorithm for binding: the agent tries credential types in order, and for each one, tries authentication methods in order, testing each server in the preferred and default lists until one succeeds. Time limits on bind and search operations are controlled by bindTimeLimit and searchTimeLimit attributes.

The agent also uses attributes like followReferrals and dereferenceAliases to control protocol behavior, and profileTTL to know when to reload the configuration. Some attributes are service-specific, like serviceAuthenticationMethod and serviceCredentialLevel, allowing different services within the same agent to have different connection settings.
sections.plainLanguage: The agent reads the profile like a recipe: 'Try these servers in order, use this login method, give up if it takes longer than this.' If the first server doesn't respond, it tries the next one from the list.

sections.title: Status and Applicability
sections.content:
This RFC is Informational, meaning it does not define an Internet Standard. It is a skeleton for future service-specific documents. The authors expected that implementing services would create additional RFCs describing how to apply this configuration schema to particular services, such as the Network Information Service (NIS) defined in RFC 2307.

The primary implementations described are from HP, PADL, and Infoblox. The schema has influenced LDAP client configuration in various Unix-based systems, though it has not become universally adopted. The core idea of storing LDAP configuration in the directory itself remains sound and is used in production environments, particularly for managing large-scale LDAP deployments where centralized configuration is valuable.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a suggestion and a blueprint, not a requirement. Different vendors can extend it for their own needs. Some systems do use it today, especially where teams need to manage many LDAP clients from one place.
